newsitem.title: LATVIA: ANALYSIS-LATVIAN SHARES IN DULL TIMES, SOME OPTIMISTIC.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS-LATVIAN SHARES IN DULL TIMES, SOME OPTIMISTIC.

text.p: The Latvian stock market has seen slow trade recently as investors neglect stocks for other areas but dealers and analysts said on Friday they were cautiously optimistic the current correction will bottom out in May.
However, they said T-bills and privatisation vouchers were strong rivals for funds.
The Riga bourse this week reached trade volumes that were close to lows registered in February at around 60,000 lats.

Analysts said the cause of the downturn was two-fold: an outflow of funds to other investments but also, more fundamentally, a lack of trust in company results and a lack of more than a handful of tradeable companies.
But Uldis Cerps, Riga stock exchange chief, was optimistic that the market would pick up steam.
"The current correction is almost complete as many companies are already showing reasonably good p/e ratios at today's price levels," he told Reuters.
Pareks Bank dealer Leonid Ruderman also saw some better acitivity in the future.
"A certain evening out of the market can be expected in May on better ratios and if there are good first quarter results," Ruderman said.
But he remained cautious on relying on first quarter figures as companies books still hide non-material assets.
These have to be paid off within five years after the privatisation and show on the books at the year-end.
"These assets were not supported by real capital during the sell-off and now have to be depreciated," he added.

Latvia's privatisation process, given new life under businessman Prime Minister Andris Shkele, is also expected to affect the market as people put money into voucher and cash privatisations and neglect already listed stocks.
"Capital accumulation of a serious size is under way," Cerps said. "Among the Baltic states, Latvia seems to engage in the widest voucher and cash privatisation in the coming two years."
Latvia has decided to sell and list stakes in important oil terminal Ventspils Nafta terminal and other key companies.
"Starting from late last week we were bombarded by clients asking for vouchers and the price jumped to 2.15-2.20 from around two lats this week," a dealer with a top bank said.
The market capitalisation of companies such as Latvian Shipping, Latvian Gas, Latvenergo and Ventpils are big, he said.

The expected market capitalisation of Ventspils Nafta is 30 million lats and that of Latvian Gas is expected to be 36 million lats. This compares with total current market capitalisation of 147 million lats.
"I would expect continued gravitating towards vouchers, which could put a cap on the bourse," the dealer added.
"The market will continue down for a short while, driven by its own momentum after dividends are paid and then will go up," said Viesturs Shterns, Unibanka's head of equities.
"Good first quarter results will definitely be able to prop the market up," he added.
The introduction of two-year government T-bills, which were first auctioned this week, are also seen by some as having led to the recent outflow of funds from equities.
But dealers said the market's problem was also due to a lack of tradeable companies in terms of size.
"There are really not more than three to four firms of a size relevant to foreign investors," said one analyst.
-- Riga Newsroom, +371 721 5240
